title: The Judge Comes from Sinai
sum: The book opens with Enoch's blessing on "the chosen and the righteous" who will live through the final day of trouble. Enoch speaks like Balaam and Moses: his eyes were opened, angels showed him a vision, and it was meant not for his own time but for a far-off generation.

Then comes the vision itself. God, "the Holy Great One," comes out of his dwelling and treads on Mount Sinai with his army. The Watchers shake, mountains melt like wax, the earth splits open, and everyone is judged. The righteous receive peace, mercy and light. The chapter ends with the verse Jude quotes: he comes with ten thousands of holy ones to judge and convict all flesh.
readings: Read as the introduction to the whole book
Chapters 1–5 were probably written as a doorway into the older stories that follow (6–36). They set the theme of all five books of 1 Enoch: a coming judgment that divides the chosen from the wicked.
Read with Jude

Jude 14–15 quotes 1:9 as Enoch's prophecy against false teachers. Reading the verse in its own setting shows that "the one who comes" is God himself, coming from Sinai; Jude applies it to the Lord Jesus.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read the chapter as Scripture: Enoch, seventh from Adam, truly prophesied the coming of the Lord, as Jude 14 says, and the church reads that coming as Christ's.
views.H: Scholars see 1–5 as a later frame, written around 200 BC or a little after, built from Deuteronomy 33, Numbers 22–24, Micah 1 and Isaiah 65. The Aramaic copy 4Q201, from the early 100s BC, already contains it.
views.N: The chapter matters for the New Testament mainly through Jude 14–15, which quotes 1:9. The picture of God coming with his holy ones also lies behind 1 Thessalonians 3:13 and Matthew 25:31, which speak of the Lord coming with his angels.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism did not keep 1 Enoch, and the rabbis rarely speak well of Enoch. But the picture of God coming from Sinai with his holy myriads is drawn straight from Deuteronomy 33:2, which Jewish tradition reads in the synagogue on Simchat Torah.
views.W: Most churches do not count 1 Enoch as Scripture but value this chapter as the source of Jude's quotation and as a witness to how Jews in Jesus' time pictured the final judgment.

deep.b:
The verse survives in four forms: the Ge'ez, the Greek of the Gizeh manuscript, a few Aramaic words from Qumran (4Q204), and Jude 14–15. Side by side: (1) "Look!" is in the Ge'ez (nahu) and Jude (idou); the Greek has "for." (2) "He has come" is past in the Ge'ez and Jude, present in the Greek. (3) "With ten thousands of holy ones": Ge'ez "with myriads of holy ones"; Greek "with his myriads and his holy ones," where Charles marks "his … and" as a corrupt addition; Jude "with his holy myriads." (4) "The Lord" is only in Jude. (5) "To carry out judgment on all" is in the Greek and Jude; the Ge'ez has "on them." (6) "Destroy the wicked" is in the Ge'ez and Greek (the Greek has "all the wicked," with no Ethiopic parallel for "all") but not in Jude. (7) "Convict all flesh": Ge'ez and Greek; Jude has "all the ungodly" or, in its oldest copies, "every soul." (8) The harsh words sinners spoke are in the Gizeh Greek, in the Aramaic as Milik read it ("great and hard"), and in Jude, but not in the Ge'ez.

The result: Jude's quotation is very close to the Greek form of the verse, shortened, with "the Lord" added. It agrees with the Ge'ez only in "look" and the past tense, which may reflect the Aramaic (Bauckham). The Plain follows the Greek where the Greek and the Aramaic agree (5, 8).

echoes: Deuteronomy 33:1–2; Numbers 24:3–4; Numbers 24:15–17; Micah 1:3–4; Habakkuk 3:3; Psalm 97:5; Numbers 6:24–26; Zechariah 14:5; Jude 14–15

settings.to: "the chosen and the righteous" of a distant generation
settings.when: the opening of the book
settings.why: To present everything that follows as Enoch's blessing for the faithful few who will live through the final crisis.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.when: said to come from before the Flood; written down, most think, around 200 BC
settings.why: To assure the faithful that God himself will come, judge the Watchers and the wicked, and give peace and light to the chosen.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

traditions.q: Jude says Enoch "prophesied" (Jude 14). Does that mean Enoch himself said these words, and what does it mean for the book?
views: Yes. An apostle calls the words prophecy and names Enoch as the speaker, so the book is Enoch's and belongs in the Bible.
The Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches read Jude without drawing that conclusion: Jude's words are true, but the book is not in their Bibles.
No. The Greek and Slavic churches do not read 1 Enoch as Scripture, though some early fathers, such as Tertullian, valued it. Jude's quotation is honored as Scripture in Jude, not in Enoch.

Jude's line is inspired, because Jude is Scripture, but the book is not. Augustine allowed that Enoch truly prophesied. Many Catholic scholars today hold that Jude quoted a respected Jewish book and called it prophecy in the way his readers did, without settling who wrote it.
Luther took the quotation as a reason to doubt Jude, not to accept Enoch: he said Jude cited a saying found nowhere in Scripture, which is why the early church had held the letter back.

The Spirit led Jude to quote a true saying, just as Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). That makes the quoted words true, not the whole book Scripture. Some Reformed writers think the prophecy may go back to the real Enoch through tradition; others think "Enoch" names the book.

Divided. Some (Schreiner, Davids) say Jude speaks as his readers did and affirms only that the prophecy came true in the false teachers; others hold that Jude, writing under inspiration, would not call it Enoch's prophecy unless it truly was, and that a genuine saying may have been kept in a later book.

title: Creation Keeps Its Order
sum: Enoch tells his hearers to look at the sky: the sun, moon and stars rise and set at their times and never break their orders. Look at the earth too, he says: nothing God made changes its nature. Summer and winter come in turn, with rain, clouds and dew.
readings: Read as a lesson from nature
The argument of 2:1–5:3 is simple: creation obeys God without fail. 5:4 will draw the contrast: everything keeps God's order except you.
Read as a calendar lesson
"In its order, at its own time" is the language of the Enoch calendar. The writers held that the sun and stars mark the true times for Israel's festivals (see 72:1).

views.E: Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read the chapter as a call to learn from creation, much as Psalm 19 does, and as a reminder that God set fixed times for worship.
views.H: Scholars compare the passage to Jeremiah 5:22–24 and 8:7, and to the Testament of Naphtali 3:2–5, which uses the same argument. It shows the Enoch group's deep interest in the order of the heavens.
views.N: Paul argues in Romans 1:20 that creation makes God's power plain, so that people are without excuse. The thought is close to this chapter.
views.J: Jewish teaching on the fixed order of nature runs from Genesis 8:22 to the daily prayer that thanks God for renewing creation each day.
views.W: Most churches can read this chapter with profit as a reflection on creation's order, in harmony with the Psalms and Jeremiah.

echoes: Psalm 19:1–6; Psalm 104:19; Jeremiah 5:22–24; Jeremiah 8:7; Genesis 8:22; Romans 1:20

settings.to: the wicked and the righteous of the last generation
settings.when: continuing the opening speech
settings.why: To show that every part of creation obeys God, so that disobedient humans have no excuse.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

title: Trees in Winter
sum: In winter nearly all trees look dead and leafless. Only fourteen keep their old leaves for two or three years until new ones come. Even the exceptions keep a rule.
readings: Read as part of the lesson
The chapter is one step in Enoch's tour of the seasons (2:1–5:3). The point is not botany but obedience: even the evergreens follow a fixed pattern.

views.E: Read with the surrounding chapters as a call to learn God's faithfulness from the natural world.
views.H: The detail of fourteen evergreen trees has no known source. The Greek copy of this passage is damaged.
views.N: Jesus also taught from trees and seasons: "learn this lesson from the fig tree" (Mark 13:28).
views.J: Later Jewish writings list trees that keep their leaves; this chapter is one of the oldest such lists, but it gives only the number.
views.W: A simple observation of nature, used to teach that God's creation is orderly.

title: Summer Heat
sum: In summer the sun stands overhead. People look for shade, the ground burns, and no one can walk on the earth or on the rocks for the heat. This too comes at its set time.
readings: Read as part of the lesson
The harsh summer of Judea is not a sign of disorder. It comes when God has set it, like everything else in 2:1–5:3.

views.E: Read with the surrounding chapters as part of Enoch's sermon on creation's obedience.
views.H: The picture fits the dry summers of the Judean hills. The Greek of 4:1 is lost from the Gizeh manuscript.
views.N: Revelation 7:16 promises that the sun's heat will no longer strike the redeemed.
views.J: The summer heat and the search for shade appear often in Jewish poetry (Isaiah 25:4; Psalm 121:6).
views.W: A reflection on the seasons that most readers can share.

title: No Peace for the Hard-Hearted
sum: Trees grow leaves and bear fruit; the seas and rivers do their work. All God's works serve him and do not change. "But you," Enoch says, "have not stood firm." The wicked have broken the Lord's commands and spoken proud, harsh words against him, so they will have no peace.

Their names will become a curse, and they will find no mercy. But the chosen will receive light, joy and peace, and will inherit the earth. Wisdom will be given to them; they will not sin again, and they will live out their days in peace.
readings: Read as a reworking of Isaiah 65
Isaiah 65 promises that God's chosen will inherit the land and live long, while rebels leave their name as a curse. 5:4–9 follows it closely.
Read as the book's first verdict
The chapter sets the two groups that run through 1 Enoch: the wicked who speak against God, and the chosen who will inherit the earth and receive wisdom.

views.E: Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read the curse on the hard-hearted and the blessing on the chosen as true prophecy of the final judgment.
views.H: Scholars note how closely 5:4–9 follows Isaiah 65:9–23 and Psalm 37, and how the Greek text of this chapter is much longer than the Ge'ez, with extra lines of blessing and curse.
views.N: "They will inherit the earth" is the promise of Matthew 5:5, and the charge of harsh words against God returns in Jude 15–16.
views.J: The contrast of the righteous who inherit the land and the wicked who are cut off is the theme of Psalm 37, which Jews read as wisdom for daily life.
views.W: Most churches can read this chapter as a call to faithfulness, in line with Psalm 37 and Jesus' beatitude, while noting that its hope is long life on earth rather than resurrection.

echoes: Isaiah 65:9; Isaiah 65:15; Isaiah 65:20–23; Psalm 37:9–11; Psalm 37:29; Matthew 5:5; Jude 15–16

settings.what: Verdict on the wicked, promise to the chosen
settings.to: the wicked, then the chosen, of the last generation
settings.when: the end of the opening speech
settings.why: To pronounce God's sentence ahead of time: no peace for those who reject God, inheritance and wisdom for the chosen.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

title: The Watchers' Oath
sum: When people had grown many, beautiful daughters were born to them. The angels, "the children of heaven," saw them, wanted them, and agreed to take wives and father children. Their leader Semyaza feared he alone would have to pay for the sin, so all of them swore an oath and bound one another with curses.

There were two hundred of them. They came down on Mount Hermon in the days of Jared, and the mountain was named for their curse-oath. The chapter ends with the names of their chiefs: nineteen in the Ge'ez, twenty-one in the Gizeh Greek and twenty in Syncellus.
readings: Read as an expansion of Genesis 6:1–4
Genesis says only that the sons of God took human wives and that the Nephilim were on earth. 1 Enoch tells it as a planned rebellion, with leaders, an oath and a place.
Read as a story about the source of evil
The Watchers' sin is the first of many in chapters 6–11. Their teaching and their sons fill the earth with violence, and the Flood follows.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox church reads the story as Scripture and as history before the Flood. Its tradition also knows the view that the "sons of God" were Seth's descendants (Asale).
views.H: Most scholars think chapters 6–11 combine two stories, one about Semyaza and the angels' marriages, one about Asael (Azazel) and forbidden teaching. They date them to the 200s BC or earlier, perhaps reflecting the wars after Alexander the Great (Nickelsburg) or quarrels about priests (Suter).
views.N: Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 refer to angels who left their place and were kept in chains for judgment, and 1 Peter 3:19–20 to spirits who disobeyed in Noah's day. Most scholars think these passages draw on this story.
views.J: Second Temple Jews such as the authors of Jubilees and the Dead Sea Scrolls accepted the angel reading. Later rabbis rejected it, reading the "sons of God" as sons of judges or nobles (Genesis Rabbah 26:5).
views.W: Most churches do not accept the story as Scripture, but study it to understand Genesis 6, Jude and 2 Peter, and to see how ancient Jews explained the spread of evil.

deep.b: In chapters 6–11 two leaders stand out. Semyaza leads the oath and the marriages, and is punished by binding for seventy generations (10:11–12). Asael, called Azazel in the Ethiopic, teaches weapons and cosmetics, and is bound in the desert (8:1; 10:4–6). Many scholars think two separate stories were joined, with a third strand about teaching magic and star-lore (8:3). The joining shows that the writers had more than one explanation for evil, and kept both.

echoes: Genesis 6:1–4; Genesis 5:18–20; Deuteronomy 3:9; Psalm 82:6–7; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4

settings.by: the narrator, quoting the angels and Semyaza
settings.to: the readers; inside the story, the angels to one another
settings.when: the days of Jared, before the Flood
settings.why: To show that the angels' sin was deliberate and shared: they knew it was a great sin and bound themselves to it.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea in the 200s BC, living under Greek kings after Alexander's wars. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as a true account of the time before the Flood.

traditions.q: Did angels really father the giants (Genesis 6:1–4)?
views: Both readings are found. The church reads 1 Enoch as Scripture, and its text makes the Watchers angels who came down to women (6:1–7:2). But according to Bruk Ayele Asale, the traditional andəmta commentary often explains the "sons of God" as children of Seth who came down from the holy mountain to the daughters of Cain, the story told in the Ethiopic Conflict of Adam and Eve. Teachers differ.
Mostly no. Ephrem the Syrian, honored across this family, taught that the "sons of God" were the sons of Seth, and that reading became common among Syriac and Coptic writers.

Most Catholic teachers since Augustine have said no. Augustine argued that the sons of God were the godly line of Seth, called "angels of God" in some copies of the Septuagint, and doubted that God's holy angels could have fallen in that way; he left open the old stories of spirits who lay with women (City of God 15.23). That became the common Catholic reading. The Church has not defined the question, and many Catholic scholars today think Genesis meant heavenly beings, told in the old language of its world. The Catechism speaks of the angels’ fall as a free choice to reject God (391–395), without tying it to Genesis 6.

Mostly no. Justin, Athenagoras and other early writers held the angel view, but from the 300s on, Eastern teachers such as John Chrysostom called it absurd to say angels married women, and read the sons of God as Seth's descendants.

Luther read the sons of God as the godly descendants of Seth, who fell by marrying for beauty and power, and the Nephilim as tyrants. Many Lutheran scholars today grant that the angel reading is the older Jewish one.

Calvin rejected the angel view as absurd and taught the Sethite view, and it became common in Reformed teaching. Some Reformed and evangelical scholars now defend the angel view instead, because Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 seem to assume it.

Divided. Many evangelical scholars and popular teachers hold the angel view, pointing to the Jewish reading in 1 Enoch, the Septuagint's "angels of God" in some copies, and Jude 6; others hold the Sethite view, or the view that the "sons of God" were kings claiming divine descent.

title: Giants on the Earth
sum: The angels took wives, slept with them and taught them potions, spells and the cutting of roots. The women gave birth to huge giants. The giants ate up everything people produced, then turned on the people themselves, and on birds, animals, reptiles and fish, eating flesh and drinking blood. Then the earth brought a charge against the lawless ones.
readings: Read as the background of the Flood
Genesis 6:11 says the earth was full of violence. 1 Enoch says where it came from: the giants.
Read as a picture of empire
Many scholars read the giants, who consume the land and its people, as the armies of Greek kings warring over Judea in the 200s BC.

views.E: Read as history: the giants of Genesis 6:4 were born of angels and women and filled the earth with violence before the Flood.
views.H: Scholars link the story to Genesis 6:4 and to the giants of Greek and Babylonian myth. The Qumran Book of Giants, a related Aramaic work, tells more about them.
views.N: The New Testament says little about giants, but 2 Peter 2:4–5 places the angels' sin right before the Flood, as here.
views.J: Jewish tradition kept stories of the giants, such as Og of Bashan, who was said to have survived the Flood. The Book of Giants and later Jewish legends grew from such stories.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an ancient Jewish way of explaining the violence before the Flood, not as part of Scripture.

settings.when: before the Flood
settings.why: To trace the world's violence and bloodshed to the angels' children, and so to justify the Flood.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea in the 200s BC, living under Greek kings after Alexander's wars. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as a true account of the time before the Flood.

title: Forbidden Knowledge
sum: Azazel taught people to make swords, knives, shields and breastplates. He showed them metals and how to work them, bracelets, jewelry, eye paint, precious stones and dyes. Wickedness and sexual sin spread. Other Watchers taught spells and root-cutting, star-reading, signs, and the paths of the moon. As people perished, their cry went up to heaven.
readings: Read as a story about culture
Weapons, makeup and astrology are pictured as gifts from rebel angels. The writers saw much of Greek civilization as dangerous knowledge.
Read beside Genesis 4
Genesis 4:17–22 gives the arts of civilization to Cain's descendants without blame. 1 Enoch gives them to angels, with blame.

views.E: Read as Scripture: knowledge used for violence and vanity comes from the fallen angels, and Christians should use God's gifts humbly.
views.H: Scholars compare Azazel to Prometheus, the Greek Titan who gave fire and crafts, and to the Babylonian sages who taught the arts before the Flood. Hanson linked Azazel to Leviticus 16.
views.N: 1 Peter 3:3 and 1 Timothy 2:9 warn against outward adornment; early Christian writers such as Tertullian used 1 Enoch 8 to argue the same point.
views.J: The scapegoat ritual of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) sends a goat "to Azazel" in the wilderness. Later Jewish tradition (for example the Talmud, Yoma 67b) connected Azazel with the fallen angels.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an ancient explanation of how human skill came to serve violence and pride, not as a teaching that crafts are evil.

settings.when: before the Flood
settings.why: To show that violence, seduction and magic come from heavenly knowledge stolen and misused.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea in the 200s BC, living under Greek kings after Alexander's wars. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as a true account of the time before the Flood.

title: The Archangels Plead
sum: Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel look down from heaven and see blood poured out on the earth. They bring the cries of the dead before God: "You are Lord of lords, God of gods and King of kings. You see everything. You have seen what Azazel taught and what Semyaza did. The giants have filled the earth with blood. The souls of the dead are crying out. You know all this, yet you tell us nothing."
readings: Read as a prayer of complaint
Like the laments of the Psalms, the prayer praises God, describes the evil and asks: why have you not acted?
Read as angels interceding
Here angels carry human cries to God. The idea appears in Tobit 12 and Revelation 8:3–4.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox church honors the archangels as intercessors, with commemorations in its Synaxarium for Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel and others (Budge). This chapter is read as a model of their prayer.
views.H: Scholars see here the first list of four archangels. The names differ between the Greek and the Ge'ez, and the Aramaic may have had Sariel.
views.N: Revelation 6:9–10 shows the souls of the slain crying "How long?" and Revelation 8:3–4 shows an angel offering prayers. Revelation 19:16 calls Christ "King of kings and Lord of lords."
views.J: Jewish tradition kept the four archangels Michael, Gabriel, Uriel and Raphael, who are later said to surround God's throne on four sides (Numbers Rabbah 2:10).
views.W: Many churches read this prayer as a picture of heaven's concern for justice. They differ on whether angels should be asked to pray for us.

echoes: Deuteronomy 10:17; Daniel 2:47; Hebrews 4:13; Revelation 6:9–10; Revelation 8:3–4; Habakkuk 1:2–4

settings.when: while the giants fill the earth with blood
settings.why: To bring the cry of the murdered before God and ask him to act.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

title: Orders from Heaven
sum: God answers by sending each archangel. Uriel warns Noah to hide from the coming flood. Raphael binds Azazel hand and foot and throws him into darkness in the desert of Dudael, under jagged rocks until the day of judgment, when he will be thrown into the fire; all sin is written against him. Gabriel sets the giants against one another so they destroy themselves. Michael binds Semyaza and his companions under the earth for seventy generations, until the final judgment and the fire.

Then God promises a renewed earth: the plant of righteousness will appear, the righteous will live long and have many children, vines and olive trees will bear abundantly, and all nations will worship God. Never again will he send a flood.
readings: Read as the pattern of judgment
The Flood and the binding of the angels are the first judgment; the fire at the end is the last. The chapter moves from one to the other without a break.
Read with Jude and 2 Peter
Angels bound in darkness until the great day (10:4–6, 12) is exactly what Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 describe.

views.E: Read as Scripture: God binds the evil powers and saves the righteous, and the new earth points to the kingdom to come.
views.H: Scholars see the binding of Azazel in the desert as built on the scapegoat rite (Leviticus 16), and the seventy generations as one of the first schemes of world history in Jewish literature.
views.N: Jude 6, 2 Peter 2:4 and 1 Peter 3:19–20 draw on this chapter. Matthew 25:41 speaks of the eternal fire "prepared for the devil and his angels," and Revelation 20:1–3 binds Satan in the abyss.
views.J: The Mishnah's account of the scapegoat pushed off a cliff (Yoma 6:6–8) is often compared with Azazel's binding. Rabbinic Judaism did not keep the Watchers' story, but medieval Jewish writers knew it.
views.W: Most churches use the chapter to understand Jude and 2 Peter and the early Jewish picture of evil powers bound until judgment.

deep.b: Each archangel has a job that matches his name or role. Uriel ("God is my light") gives Noah the knowledge to survive. Raphael ("God heals") binds Azazel so the earth can be healed (10:7). Gabriel ("God is my strength") turns the giants' strength against themselves. Michael, the leader of heaven's army in Daniel and Revelation, binds the Watchers' leader. The scene answers the prayer of chapter 9 point by point.

echoes: Genesis 6:8–22; Genesis 9:11; Leviticus 16:8–10; Leviticus 16:21–22; Isaiah 24:21–22; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4; 1 Peter 3:19–20; Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:1–3

settings.when: before the Flood
settings.why: To save Noah and his descendants from the coming flood.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.when: before the Flood
settings.why: To bind the rebel angels, destroy the giants and cleanse the earth.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.what: The promise of a renewed earth
settings.to: Michael, and through him the readers
settings.when: spoken before the Flood, about the end
settings.why: To give hope that after judgment the earth will be made righteous and fruitful.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea in the 200s BC, who longed for a world without violence. Christians later read it as a picture of Christ's kingdom (Irenaeus).

traditions.q: Who were the "spirits in prison" of 1 Peter 3:19?
views: The Catechism teaches that Christ descended to the dead to free the righteous who had gone before him (Catechism 632–635), and reads 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 in that light.
Christ went down to Hades and preached to the dead, breaking its gates; Holy Saturday and the icon of the Resurrection celebrate this "harrowing of hell."
Christ descended to Sheol and freed the souls held there. The church also reads 1 Enoch's account of the imprisoned Watchers as true, and some teachers connect the two.
The Formula of Concord confesses that Christ descended into hell to proclaim his victory over the devil, not to suffer or offer a second chance.

Divided. Calvin read the passage as Christ's grace made known to the souls of the dead (Institutes 2.16.9). Some Reformed writers, such as Theodore Beza, John Owen and Matthew Poole, and later Wayne Grudem, read it as Christ preaching through Noah to the people of Noah's day, a view Augustine had proposed.
Divided. Many scholars now read the spirits as the fallen angels of 1 Enoch, to whom Christ announced his victory; others hold the preaching-through-Noah view.

title: A World of Peace
sum: God promises to open the storehouses of blessing in heaven and send them down on the earth and on the works of human hands. Peace and truth will be partners for all the days of the world and all its generations.
readings: Read as the end of the Flood story
The cycle of 6–11 ends where it began, on earth, but now with blessing instead of blood.

views.E: Read as a promise of the peace of God's kingdom.
views.H: The two verses close the unit 6–11. Their hope is for a renewed earth, not heaven.
views.N: The hope for a world where peace and truth meet appears in Jesus' preaching of the kingdom and in Revelation 21:1–4.
views.J: The words echo Psalm 85:10–11 and Deuteronomy 28:12, verses Jews read as promises of blessing in the land.
views.W: A short hymn of hope that most readers can share.

settings.to: Michael, and through him the readers
settings.when: spoken before the Flood, about the end
settings.why: To close God's answer (10:1–11:2) with blessing from heaven and lasting peace.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea in the 200s BC, who longed for a world without violence.

title: Enoch the Scribe
sum: Before all this Enoch had been hidden, and no one knew where he was: he was with the holy ones and the Watchers. While Enoch was blessing the great Lord, the Watchers of heaven called him, "Enoch the scribe," and sent him to the fallen Watchers. He is to tell them that because they left high heaven and made themselves unclean with women, they will have no peace and no forgiveness. They will see their beloved children killed and will plead forever without mercy.
readings: Read as Enoch's call
Chapters 12–16 tell how Enoch became a prophet to the fallen angels. Here the holy angels give him his first message.
Read as a picture of priests
The language of leaving the holy place and becoming unclean is the language of priests. Some scholars think the story criticizes priests of the writers' own day.

views.E: Read as Scripture: Enoch, who walked with God, was sent with God's judgment to the angels who sinned.
views.H: Scholars see 12–16 as a separate story from 6–11, written to explain how Enoch knew about the Watchers. It may have taken shape in the area around Mount Hermon (Nickelsburg).
views.N: Jude 6 speaks of the angels who left their own dwelling. Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was taken "so that he did not see death."
views.J: Genesis 5:24's "Enoch walked with God" is explained here as Enoch living with the angels. Later Jewish mystical writings, such as 3 Enoch, make Enoch into the angel Metatron.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an ancient Jewish explanation of Genesis 5:24 and background to Jude 6.

settings.when: while Enoch is hidden with the angels, before the Flood
settings.why: To send Enoch to the fallen Watchers with the sentence that they will have no peace or forgiveness.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).
views: Most scholars place the writers in Judea. Nickelsburg argued that chapters 12–16 took shape around Dan and Mount Hermon in Upper Galilee, where visionaries sought revelations; others think the northern setting is only part of the story.

title: The Watchers' Petition
sum: Enoch tells Azazel that he will have no peace: a great judgment has gone out against him, and he will be bound. Then Enoch goes to all the Watchers. They are terrified and ask him to write a petition so that they may be forgiven, for they are too ashamed to speak to God themselves. Enoch writes it, goes to the waters of Dan near Mount Hermon, and reads it until he falls asleep. In a dream he sees visions of punishment. He wakes, finds the Watchers mourning between Lebanon and Senir, and tells them what he saw.
readings: Read as a prophet's task reversed
Usually angels bring messages to humans. Here a human carries the angels' prayer to God, and then God's answer back to them.
Read as a story set in a real place
The springs of Dan and the slopes of Hermon were holy places in the writers' day. The story may claim that ground for Israel's God.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the fallen angels' prayer is refused because they sinned with full knowledge, and Enoch is God's faithful messenger.
views.H: Nickelsburg argued that the setting near Dan and Hermon shows that the story was shaped in northern Galilee, a region with a history of visions. Others are less sure.
views.N: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi took place near the same spot (Matthew 16:13–19). 1 Peter 3:19 speaks of a proclamation to imprisoned spirits.
views.J: Dan was the site of Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kings 12:29), and Jewish tradition remembered it as a place of false worship.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as background to 1 Peter 3:19 and Jude 6, not as Scripture.

settings.when: after Enoch's commission (12:3–6)
settings.why: To announce Azazel's binding and the refusal of mercy.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.to: the readers; inside the story, the Watchers and then God
settings.when: after the Watchers are condemned
settings.why: To show that the Watchers asked for forgiveness and that God answered through a dream.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).
views: Most scholars place the writers in Judea. Nickelsburg argued that chapters 12–16 took shape around Dan and Mount Hermon in Upper Galilee, where visionaries sought revelations; others think the northern setting is only part of the story.

title: Up to the Throne
sum: Enoch writes "the book of the words of righteousness and of the rebuke of the Watchers." He tells them that their petition is refused: they will never go up to heaven again, and they will see their sons die. Then he describes his vision. Clouds and winds carried him up to heaven. He passed a wall of hailstones and tongues of fire, entered a great house of hail and fire, and then saw a second, greater house built of fire.

Inside was a high throne like frost, with wheels like the sun and the sound of cherubim. Rivers of fire flowed from under it. The Great Glory sat on it, his robe brighter than the sun and whiter than snow. No angel could look at his face. Myriads stood before him, yet he needed no counsel. Enoch lay face down, trembling, until the Lord called him: "Come here, Enoch, and hear my holy word."
readings: Read as the first heavenly journey
Isaiah and Ezekiel saw God; Enoch is carried up to him. This is the oldest Jewish account of a human ascending to God's throne.
Read as a temple vision
The wall, the outer house and the inner house match the parts of the temple. Heaven is God's true sanctuary, and the angels are its priests.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox church reads the vision as a true revelation of God's throne, in harmony with Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1, Daniel 7 and Revelation 4.
views.H: Scholars rank 1 Enoch 14 as a founding text of Jewish throne-mysticism. It is probably older than Daniel 7, which shares the throne with wheels, the river of fire, the white garment and the myriads (Nickelsburg; Himmelfarb).
views.N: Revelation 4–5 has a throne, fire, a sea like crystal, living creatures and myriads of angels. Hebrews 8–9 speaks of the heavenly sanctuary. Paul was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2–4).
views.J: Jewish Merkavah ("chariot") mysticism, from the Dead Sea Scrolls' Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice to the Hekhalot writings, describes heavenly palaces in ways that grow from this chapter.
views.W: Most churches read the vision as a remarkable early Jewish picture of God's holiness, close to Isaiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, though not itself Scripture.

deep.b: Enoch's throne vision stands between Ezekiel's and Daniel's. From Ezekiel 1 and 10 it takes the cherubim, the wheels, the fire and the brightness. With Daniel 7:9–10 it shares the white garment, the flaming throne with wheels, the river of fire and the myriads before him. Since the Aramaic copies of 1 Enoch 1–36 are as old as Daniel or older, most scholars think Daniel knew this vision or a source shared with it. Revelation 4 then draws on all three.

echoes: Isaiah 6:1–5; Ezekiel 1:4–28; Ezekiel 10:1–22; Daniel 7:9–10; 1 Kings 6:1–29; Revelation 4:1–11; Revelation 5:11; 2 Corinthians 12:2–4

settings.when: after the dream at Dan
settings.why: To announce that their petition is refused and they will never return to heaven.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.when: the dream at Dan (13:7–8)
settings.why: To show that the verdict comes from God himself, whose holiness no angel can approach.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).
views: Most scholars place the writers in Judea. Nickelsburg argued that chapters 12–16 took shape around Dan and Mount Hermon in Upper Galilee, where visionaries sought revelations; others think the northern setting is only part of the story.

title: God's Answer to the Watchers
sum: God speaks to Enoch in his own voice: "Do not be afraid, righteous man and scribe of righteousness. Tell the Watchers: you should be pleading for human beings, not humans for you." They were holy, spiritual and immortal, yet they left heaven, made themselves unclean with women and fathered giants. God gave wives to mortals so their race could go on, but the spirits of heaven need no wives, for they never die.

Now the giants, born of spirit and flesh, will be evil spirits on the earth. Their spirits came out of their bodies. They trouble, destroy and fight, they eat nothing and cannot be seen, and they rise up against human beings, from whom they came.
readings: Read as an explanation of demons
The chapter answers a question the Bible leaves open: where do evil spirits come from? They are the ghosts of the giants.
Read as a lesson about boundaries
Heaven and earth each have their own kind of life. The Watchers' sin was to mix them, and the result was spirits that belong nowhere.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the evil spirits that trouble people are the spirits of the giants, who will be judged at the end, and Christ's power drives them out.
views.H: Scholars see 15:8–16:1 as the earliest Jewish account of the origin of demons, developed further in Jubilees 10 and in Qumran prayers against "the spirits of the bastards" (4Q510–511).
views.N: The Gospels are full of unclean spirits that seek bodies (Mark 5:1–13; Luke 11:24–26). Jesus' words that angels do not marry because they do not die (Luke 20:35–36) use the same reasoning as 15:4–7.
views.J: Later rabbis gave other accounts of demons (for example that they were created at twilight on the sixth day, Mishnah Avot 5:6 and Genesis Rabbah 7:5), but the giants' spirits appear in some Jewish magic texts.
views.W: Most churches teach that demons are fallen angels (Revelation 12:9) and read 1 Enoch's view as an ancient Jewish alternative, useful for understanding the Gospels' world.

echoes: Luke 20:34–36; Matthew 22:30; Mark 1:23–27; Mark 5:1–13; Luke 11:24–26; Genesis 6:4

settings.to: Enoch, to carry back to the fallen Watchers
settings.when: in the heavenly vision (14:24–25)
settings.why: To refuse the Watchers' petition and explain where evil spirits come from and how long they may act.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who studied the heavens and the law and expected God to judge a violent world. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

views: The church reads 1 Enoch as Scripture and so accepts that evil spirits came from the giants, alongside the fall of Satan and his angels.
Demons are angels created good who freely chose to reject God (Catechism 391–395). The Church does not teach that they were giants' spirits.
Demons are fallen angels who followed the devil in his pride. Early writers such as Justin and Athenagoras had linked them with the Watchers' children, but this view was later dropped.
Demons are fallen angels under Satan; their origin matters less than Christ's authority over them, which believers exercise in his name (Mark 16:17).
Most say demons are the angels who fell with Satan (Revelation 12:9). Some scholars note that 1 Enoch's view was common among Jews in Jesus' day.

title: A Worthless Secret
sum: From the day the giants died, their spirits will go on destroying, without judgment, until the great day of the end. As for the Watchers who sent Enoch to plead for them, he is to say: "You were in heaven, but its secrets had not been revealed to you. You knew a worthless secret and told it to the women, and through it women and men do more and more evil on earth. You will have no peace."
readings: Read as the end of God's answer
The chapter closes the speech of 15:1–16:4 with the refrain heard since 5:4: no peace.
Read as a lesson about knowledge
The Watchers' knowledge was partial and cheap, yet it did great harm. Real wisdom comes from God's revelation.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the devil's knowledge is a counterfeit wisdom that leads people to sin.
views.H: Scholars note the contrast between the Watchers' worthless secrets and the true mysteries given to Enoch. The theme runs through all of 1 Enoch.
views.N: Paul contrasts the wisdom of this age with God's hidden wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:6–8), and 1 Peter 1:12 says angels long to look into the gospel.
views.J: Deuteronomy 29:29 separates the hidden things of God from what he has revealed to Israel, a verse Jews read as a guide to the limits of knowledge.
views.W: Most readers can take the chapter as a warning that knowledge without God harms, without accepting its account of the Watchers.

title: Enoch's First Journey
sum: The angels take Enoch to a place where beings like blazing fire can look like men. He sees a mountain reaching to heaven, the places of the lights and the thunder, a bow of fire with arrows, a sword of fire, and lightning. He sees the water of life, the fire of the west that receives the setting sun, a river of fire flowing into the great sea, the great rivers, the great darkness, the mountains of winter, and the mouths of all the rivers and of the deep.
readings: Read as a tour of the ends of the earth
Chapters 17–19 are the first of Enoch's journeys, to the far west and the edge of the world.
Read as God's armory
The bow, arrows, sword and lightning are the weapons God uses in the Psalms and prophets (Psalm 18:14; Habakkuk 3:9–11).

views.E: Read as a true vision of the hidden parts of creation, showing God's power over all things.
views.H: Scholars compare the geography with Greek pictures of the underworld (the river of fire Pyriphlegethon, the ocean at the edge) and with Babylonian maps. Bautch thinks the writers used a shared Near Eastern world picture.
views.N: Revelation also pictures fire, water of life and the abyss (Revelation 20:10; 22:1).
views.J: Jewish tradition kept a lively interest in the "works of creation" (ma'aseh bereshit), but the Mishnah limited teaching about it (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1).
views.W: Most readers take the journeys as an ancient religious map of the world, not as geography.

settings.to: the readers (he is speaking after the vision of 14–16)
settings.when: after God's answer to the Watchers
settings.why: To show that God has places of punishment ready at the ends of the earth, and that the Watchers' doom is certain.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Prison at the End of the World
sum: Enoch sees the storehouses of the winds, the cornerstone of the earth, and the four winds that hold up the earth and the dome of the sky. In the south he sees seven mountains of precious stone; the middle one reaches to heaven like God's throne, of a stone called peka with a top of sapphire. Beyond lies a deep chasm with pillars of fire, and beyond that a desert place with no sky above and no ground below.

There he sees seven stars like great burning mountains. The angel explains that this is the end of heaven and earth, a prison for the stars who broke God's command by not rising at their proper times. They are bound for ten thousand years.
readings: Read with Job 38
Enoch is shown the very things God asks Job about: the storehouses of the winds and the earth's cornerstone.
Read with the calendar
The punished stars failed to rise on time, a warning to people who keep the wrong calendar.

views.E: Read as Scripture: God's order rules even the stars, and those who rebel are punished.
views.H: Scholars see in the disobedient stars both fallen angels and the Enoch group's concern for the right calendar (see 72:1). The seven mountains reappear in 24–25.
views.N: Jude 13's "wandering stars" kept for darkness and Revelation's stars that fall from heaven (Revelation 8:10; 9:1) fit this picture.
views.J: The idea that stars are living beings who can be judged is found in Job 38:7 and Isaiah 24:21–23, which Jewish readers knew well.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as poetry about God's rule over creation and background to Jude 13.

echoes: Job 38:4–7; Job 38:22; Psalm 135:7; Isaiah 24:21–22; Isaiah 54:11; Jude 13

settings.what: The angel explains the prison of the stars
settings.when: on the first journey
settings.why: To show that disobedience in heaven is punished, so that the readers will trust God's order.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Fate of the Angels
sum: Uriel tells Enoch that here the angels who mingled with women will stand. Their spirits take many forms, ruin people, and lead them to sacrifice to demons as to gods, until the great day of judgment. Their wives will become sirens. Enoch says that he alone saw these sights, the ends of everything; no one else will see what he has seen.
readings: Read as the end of the first journey
The journey that began in 17:1 ends at the prison of the angels, and Enoch closes it with a claim to unique sight.
Read as a teaching about idols
Pagan worship is pictured as worship of the Watchers' spirits, as Deuteronomy 32:17 and 1 Corinthians 10:20 also say.

views.E: Read as Scripture: idolatry is worship of demons, and Enoch is the unique witness of God's hidden works.
views.H: Scholars note that the Greek and Ge'ez differ on whether the women led the angels astray; the Greek is probably older. "Sirens" may come from the Greek Old Testament's word for desert creatures.
views.N: Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20), and John 3:13 says no one has gone up to heaven except the Son of Man.
views.J: Jewish teaching from Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37 identified foreign gods with demons.
views.W: Most churches accept the chapter's view that idols have demonic power behind them, which Paul shares, but not its claims about Enoch.

settings.when: at the end of the first journey
settings.why: To show where the rebel angels will be held, and why their spirits still lead people into false worship.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Seven Archangels
sum: A list of the holy angels who keep watch, each with his charge: Uriel over the world and Tartarus; Raphael over human spirits; Raguel, who takes vengeance on the world and the lights; Michael over the best of humankind, the people of Israel; Saraqael over spirits who sin; Gabriel over the serpents, the garden and the cherubim; and, in the Greek, Remiel over those who rise.
readings: Read as the guide list for the journeys
These angels are Enoch's guides in chapters 21–36: Uriel, Raphael, Raguel and Michael speak to him in turn.
Read with Tobit and Revelation
"Seven angels who stand before God" appear in Tobit 12:15 and Revelation 8:2.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox church honors these archangels by name, including Uriel (Urael) and Raguel, and its Synaxarium (Sənkəssar) lists their commemorations through the year (Budge).
views.H: Scholars see the list as a later addition that names the guides of 21–36. The Ge'ez has six names, the Greek seven.
views.N: Revelation 8:2 has seven angels who stand before God; Michael and Gabriel are named in Jude 9, Revelation 12:7 and Luke 1:19.
views.J: Jewish tradition kept the four great angels and sometimes seven. Outside 1 Enoch, Sariel is named in the War Scroll from Qumran (1QM 9:15); the other names here are known mainly from the Enoch tradition itself.
views.W: Most churches name only Michael, Gabriel and, in Catholic and Orthodox use, Raphael. A Roman decree of 745 warned against invoking other angel names.

echoes: Tobit 12:15; Revelation 8:2; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 12:1; Luke 1:19; Jude 9; 2 Peter 2:4

traditions.q: May Christians honor angels by names not found in the 66 books?
views: Yes. The church honors Uriel (Urael), Raguel, Phanuel and others named in 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra alongside Michael and Gabriel, and its Synaxarium keeps monthly commemorations of the archangels, such as Michael on the 12th and Gabriel on the 19th of each month.

Yes, within limits. The feast of 8 November is the Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the other bodiless powers, and Orthodox tradition and icons of the feast commonly name seven archangels: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, Selaphiel, Jegudiel and Barachiel. Gabriel also has his own feasts (26 March and 13 July).

Only Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, who are named in Scripture (Raphael in Tobit). A Roman council in 745 rejected prayers to Uriel and other names, and the Vatican's 2001 directory on popular piety repeats the caution. The Church keeps one feast of Michael, Gabriel and Raphael on 29 September.
Michael and all angels are remembered on September 29, but angels are not prayed to, and only biblical names are used.
No. Christians should not pray to angels at all, and names outside Scripture are speculation (Calvin, Institutes 1.14.8).

title: Two Prisons
sum: Enoch travels to a place where nothing has been made: no sky above and no ground below. There seven stars of heaven are bound together like burning mountains. Uriel explains that they broke the command of God Most High and are bound for ten thousand ages. Then Enoch sees a place more terrible still: a cleft going down to the deep, full of great pillars of falling fire, beyond measuring. "This place is the prison of the angels," Uriel says. "They will be held here forever."
readings: Read as the start of the second journey
Chapters 21–36 retrace the ground of 17–19 more fully, with an angel explaining each sight.
Read with Jude and 2 Peter
The prison of the angels is the place Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 describe: chains, darkness, kept for judgment.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the prison of the angels is real, and God's justice reaches even the heavenly rebels.
views.H: Scholars see in 21 a doublet of 18:10–19:2, perhaps from a second hand. The Greek "unformed" place recalls Genesis 1:2.
views.N: 2 Peter 2:4's "Tartarus" and Jude 6's "everlasting chains" fit this chapter; 1 Peter 3:19's "spirits in prison" may too.
views.J: The idea of a prison for heavenly rebels appears in Isaiah 24:21–22, which says the host of heaven will be shut up in a prison and punished after many days.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as background to Jude, 2 Peter and Revelation's abyss.

echoes: Isaiah 24:21–22; Genesis 1:2; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4; Revelation 9:1–2; Revelation 20:1–3

settings.when: on the second journey
settings.why: To let Enoch ask what the readers would ask (21:4, 8) and to show the difference between the stars' prison, which has an end, and the angels' prison, which lasts forever.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Places of the Dead
sum: In the west Enoch sees a great mountain of hard rock with four hollow places, deep and dark. Raphael explains that the souls of the dead are gathered there until the day of judgment. Enoch hears the spirit of Abel, still pleading against Cain until Cain's descendants are gone.

Raphael explains the divisions: one place for the righteous, with a bright spring of water; one for sinners who were never judged in life, who suffer until the great day; one for the murdered, who plead for justice; and one for sinners who will stay there and not be raised. Enoch blesses the Lord of glory.
readings: Read as the first map of the afterlife
Older biblical texts send all the dead to Sheol alike. Here the dead are separated by how they lived, long before the final judgment.
Read with Luke 16
The bright spring for the righteous and the pain for sinners, with a gulf between, is close to Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the souls of the dead wait in separate places until the resurrection, and the prayers and good works of the living matter for them.
views.H: Scholars see chapter 22 as a key witness to the growth of Jewish ideas about the afterlife between Ecclesiastes and Daniel 12. The numbers do not quite fit (four hollows in 22:2, "these three" in 22:9); the Gizeh Greek's extra line, three dark hollows and one bright, may be the writer's own way of joining them, or a sign that the text grew in stages.
views.N: Luke 16:19–31 has a divided underworld; Revelation 6:9–10 has the souls of martyrs crying out; Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Abel's blood.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism later spoke of Gan Eden and Gehinnom as places of reward and purification after death, and of the righteous and wicked waiting for the resurrection.
views.W: Many churches find here an early form of the belief in an intermediate state, which they understand in different ways.

deep.h: Who is in the four hollows?
deep.b: Raphael names four groups (22:9–13): (1) the righteous, with the spring of light; (2) sinners who escaped judgment in life, held in pain for the great day; (3) the murdered, like Abel, who plead for vengeance; (4) sinners who were already punished or who sided with the wicked, who will not be raised. The Gizeh Greek adds that three hollows are dark and one is bright, with a spring (see the variant at 22:2). The scheme answers a pressing question: what happens to those whose lives ended without justice? The answer is that God keeps every case open until the judgment.

echoes: Genesis 4:8–10; Psalm 88:10–12; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Daniel 12:2; Luke 16:19–31; Hebrews 12:24; Revelation 6:9–10

settings.what: Raphael explains the places of the dead
settings.when: on the second journey, in the far west
settings.why: To show that God keeps every soul until judgment and that no injustice is forgotten.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

settings.what: Enoch blesses the Lord of glory
settings.when: after the vision of the dead
settings.why: To respond to God's justice with praise.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

traditions.q: Do the dead wait in an in-between state before the final judgment?
views: Yes. Souls face a particular judgment at death; the righteous are with God, some are purified in purgatory, and the lost are separated from God, until the resurrection of the body (Catechism 1021–1037).
Yes. The souls of the dead have a foretaste of joy or sorrow before the last judgment, and the church prays for the departed.
Yes. Souls wait in places of rest or pain until the resurrection; prayers and memorial services help the departed. 1 Enoch 22 is read in this light.
Believers who die are with Christ (Philippians 1:23), awaiting the resurrection; there is no purgatory.
No conscious in-between state. The dead sleep until the resurrection (Ecclesiastes 9:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–16).
No. The dead are unconscious and await a resurrection; there is no immortal soul.

title: The Restless Fire
sum: Enoch goes west to the ends of the earth and sees a fire that runs without rest, day and night. Raguel explains that it is the fire of all the lights of heaven.
readings: Read as part of the order of the heavens
The lights of the sky need a source; the writers place it in a restless fire in the west.

views.E: Read as a sign of God's constant care for the lights of heaven.
views.H: Scholars compare the passage with ancient ideas about what moves the stars. Raguel, "friend of God," is the angel who punishes the lights (20:4).
views.N: James 1:17 calls God "the Father of lights, with whom there is no change."
views.J: Jewish morning prayers bless God as the one who forms light and renews creation each day.
views.W: A short scene of ancient cosmology, read as poetry about God's ordering of the world.

settings.when: on the second journey
settings.why: To show that even the fire that drives the lights serves God.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Mountain Throne
sum: Enoch sees a mountain of fire and seven glorious mountains of precious stone, three to the east and three to the south, with deep valleys between. The seventh stands in the middle like the seat of a throne, surrounded by fragrant trees. Among them is one tree unlike any other: its scent is sweeter than all, its leaves and blossoms never wither, and its fruit is like clusters of dates. Michael, who is with him, answers his wonder.
readings: Read as a vision of God's mountain
The throne mountain joins Sinai, Zion and the mountain of God in Ezekiel 28.
Read as the tree of life
The unnamed tree is the tree of life, guarded since Eden, waiting for the righteous.

views.E: Read as a vision of paradise and of the tree of life, which Christians receive through Christ.
views.H: Scholars place the seven mountains in the far northwest of the known world and compare them with Ezekiel 28:13–16 and Isaiah 14:13.
views.N: Revelation 22:2 places the tree of life in the new Jerusalem; Revelation 2:7 promises it to the one who overcomes.
views.J: Jewish tradition held that the tree of life was kept for the righteous in the world to come.
views.W: Most readers can read the chapter as a picture of the hope that Eden will be restored.

echoes: Genesis 2:9; Ezekiel 28:13–16; Isaiah 14:13; Psalm 48:1–2; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2

title: Fruit for the Chosen
sum: Michael explains: the high mountain is God's throne, where the Holy Great One, the Lord of glory, the eternal King, will sit when he comes down to visit the earth with goodness. No one may touch the fragrant tree until the great judgment. Then it will be given to the righteous and humble; its fruit will give life to the chosen, and it will be planted by the house of the Lord. They will live long lives, as their fathers did, with no sorrow or plague. Enoch blesses the Lord of glory.
readings: Read with Revelation 22
The tree of life replanted by God's house for the righteous is the hope of Revelation 22:1–2, 14.
Read as a hope for the land
The tree is planted in Jerusalem, and the reward is long life on earth: an earthly hope, as in Isaiah 65.

views.E: Read as Scripture: the tree of life is a promise fulfilled in Christ and given to the faithful in the kingdom.
views.H: Scholars note that the reward is long earthly life, not eternal life; the Book of the Watchers stands before the resurrection became central.
views.N: Revelation 2:7 and 22:2, 14 promise the tree of life to the faithful. 1 Timothy 1:17 calls God "the King of the ages."
views.J: Later Jewish writings say the tree of life will be given to the righteous in the world to come; the temple was seen as a new Eden.
views.W: Most churches can read the chapter as a witness to the hope of restored paradise, in a form older than the New Testament's.

echoes: Genesis 3:22–24; Isaiah 65:20–22; Ezekiel 47:12; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2; Revelation 22:14

settings.when: on the second journey
settings.why: To promise that the tree of life, closed since Eden, will be given to the righteous after the judgment.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

settings.when: after Michael's words
settings.why: To praise God for what he has prepared for the righteous.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Center of the Earth
sum: Enoch goes to the middle of the earth and sees a blessed, fertile place, with branches growing from a felled tree. There is a holy mountain with water flowing south from its east side, a higher mountain to the east, a lower one to the west, and deep, narrow valleys between them.
readings: Read as a map of Jerusalem
The holy mountain is Zion, the spring is the Gihon, the eastern mountain is the Mount of Olives, and the valleys are the Kidron and Hinnom.

views.E: Read as a vision of Jerusalem, the holy city at the center of the world.
views.H: Scholars match the description closely to Jerusalem's landscape, which suggests the writers knew the city well.
views.N: Revelation 21–22 makes the new Jerusalem the center of the new creation.
views.J: Jewish tradition calls Jerusalem the navel of the world (Jubilees 8:19; Ezekiel 38:12), and later the temple's foundation stone was said to be the world's center.
views.W: A description of Jerusalem in the language of sacred geography.

title: The Cursed Valley
sum: Enoch asks why this land is blessed while the valley is cursed. Uriel answers that the cursed valley is for those cursed forever, who speak against God and his glory. There they will be gathered and judged, and in the last days the righteous will see their judgment and bless the Lord of glory for his mercy. Enoch blesses God.
readings: Read as the origin of Gehenna
The valley beside Jerusalem is the Valley of Hinnom, which became the name for hell in the New Testament.
Read as judgment for speech
Once again the sin named is harsh words against God (5:4; 1:9).

views.E: Read as Scripture: the place of final punishment is real, and the righteous will praise God's mercy and justice.
views.H: Scholars see here the earliest text that makes the Valley of Hinnom a place of final judgment, building on Jeremiah 7:31–32 and Isaiah 66:24.
views.N: Jesus speaks of Gehenna as the place of final punishment (Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43–48), quoting Isaiah 66:24.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism made Gehinnom the place of purification and punishment after death, usually for a limited time (Mishnah Eduyot 2:10 speaks of twelve months).
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early witness to the idea of Gehenna, which Jesus took up.

echoes: 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32; Isaiah 66:24; Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43–48; Jude 15

settings.when: on the second journey, at Jerusalem
settings.why: To show where those who curse God will be judged, in sight of the righteous.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

settings.what: Enoch blesses the Lord of glory
settings.when: after Uriel's words about the cursed valley
settings.why: To answer the sight of judgment with praise of God's greatness.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: Into the Desert
sum: Enoch goes east into the mountains of the desert and sees a lonely wilderness, yet full of trees and plants, with water gushing from above and a great stream flowing toward the northwest.
readings: Read as the road east
The journey now runs east from Jerusalem through the Judean desert, toward paradise.

views.E: Read as part of Enoch's journey to paradise.
views.H: The Greek keeps the Aramaic word for "desert" as a place name, Mandobara. The landscape fits the desert east of Jerusalem.
views.N: Jesus was tested in this desert (Mark 1:12–13).
views.J: Isaiah 35:1–7 and Ezekiel 47 promise that the desert will bloom and fresh water will flow to the Dead Sea.
views.W: A scene of desert made fruitful, read as a picture of God's renewal.

title: Trees of Fragrance
sum: Further east, near the mountains, Enoch sees trees giving out the scent of frankincense and myrrh.
readings: Read as the spice road
Chapters 29–32 follow the spices of the temple incense toward the east.

views.E: Read as part of the journey to paradise; the spices are those of worship.
views.H: The phrase "trees of judgment" is obscure in both the Ge'ez and the Greek.
views.N: The magi brought frankincense and myrrh to Jesus (Matthew 2:11).
views.J: Frankincense was part of the holy incense of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:34).
views.W: A detail of the spice-filled road to paradise.

title: Cinnamon and Mastic
sum: Beyond the eastern mountains Enoch sees valleys of water that never run dry, a beautiful tree with a scent like mastic, and fragrant cinnamon along the valleys.
readings: Read as the spice road
Each step east brings a new fragrance, a sign of approaching paradise.

views.E: Read as part of Enoch's journey east.
views.H: Cinnamon and mastic were luxury trade goods from the east and from the Aegean.
views.N: Revelation 18:13 lists cinnamon among the trade goods of Babylon.
views.J: Cinnamon was part of the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).
views.W: A brief scene on the way to the garden.

title: Nectar and Aloes
sum: Enoch sees a mountain whose trees pour out a nectar called sarira and galbanum, and another with aloe trees bearing hard fruit like almonds, which smells sweeter than any perfume.
readings: Read as the spice road
Galbanum was part of the temple incense; the road east is lined with the materials of worship.

views.E: Read as part of Enoch's journey east.
views.H: The spices match lists in Exodus 30 and Sirach 24:15.
views.N: Nicodemus brought aloes for Jesus' burial (John 19:39).
views.J: Galbanum's sharp smell in the holy incense was later said by the rabbis to show that sinners belong in the community's prayer (Talmud, Keritot 6b).
views.W: A brief scene of fragrant trees.

title: The Garden of Righteousness
sum: Enoch passes seven mountains full of nard, cinnamon and pepper, crosses the Red Sea, and passes the angel Zotiel. He comes to the Garden of Righteousness, with great and beautiful trees, and sees the tree of wisdom, whose eaters gain great wisdom. It looks like a carob, with fruit like grapes. Raphael tells him that his first father and mother ate from it, learned wisdom, saw that they were naked, and were driven out of the garden.
readings: Read as Eden revisited
The journey east ends in the garden of Genesis 2, and Raphael tells the story of Genesis 3 in a few words.
Read with chapter 24
There are two trees: the tree of life on God's mountain (24–25) and the tree of wisdom in the garden (32).

views.E: Read as Scripture: paradise still exists, and the righteous will return to it through Christ.
views.H: Scholars note that the Book of the Watchers mentions Adam and Eve only here and places the main origin of evil with the Watchers. The garden lies in the far east, as Genesis 2:8 says.
views.N: Jesus promises paradise to the thief (Luke 23:43); Paul was caught up to paradise (2 Corinthians 12:4).
views.J: Jewish tradition calls paradise Gan Eden, the place where the righteous dead rest.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a retelling of Genesis 2–3 and a witness to the Jewish belief in a garden of the righteous.

echoes: Genesis 2:8–17; Genesis 3:6–7; Genesis 3:22–24; Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7

settings.what: Raphael on the tree of wisdom
settings.when: at the end of the journey east
settings.why: To connect Enoch's journey with the story of Eden.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The Gates of Heaven
sum: At the ends of the earth Enoch sees great beasts and birds of every kind. East of them, where the sky rests on the earth, the gates of heaven stand open. He watches the stars come out and writes down their gates, numbers, names, orders, positions, times and months, as Uriel shows him. Uriel writes them down too.
readings: Read as a bridge to the Book of the Luminaries
Enoch the scribe begins to record the stars, the subject of chapters 72–82.

views.E: Read as Scripture: Enoch received knowledge of the heavens from God's angel, which the church's calendar tradition honors.
views.H: Scholars see 33–36 as a summary of the astronomy in 72–82, written in the same tradition.
views.N: The New Testament says little about astronomy, but Genesis 1:14 says the lights are for signs and seasons.
views.J: Jubilees 4:17 says Enoch wrote down the signs of heaven so that people might know the seasons.
views.W: A brief scene that introduces the Enochic calendar.

settings.when: at the eastern ends of the earth
settings.why: To present Enoch's books on the stars as written under an angel's guidance.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.

title: The North Winds
sum: In the north Enoch sees three gates of heaven. Through one the wind blows for good; through the other two it blows with force and brings cold, hail, frost, snow, dew and rain, and hardship comes on the earth.
readings: Read as part of the four directions
Chapters 33–36 go round the edges of the world: east, north, west, south, and east again.

views.E: Read as a sign of God's rule over the weather.
views.H: The scene is a short version of 76:1–14 on the twelve gates of the winds.
views.N: Revelation 7:1 pictures four angels holding back the four winds of the earth.
views.J: Job 37:9 says cold comes from the north, and the Psalms praise God for snow and frost.
views.W: A brief poem about the winds.

title: The West
sum: In the west Enoch sees three open gates of heaven, the same number as in the east.
readings: Read as part of the four directions
One sentence completes the western side of the circuit.

views.E: Read as part of Enoch's survey of the heavens.
views.H: The verse is a brief link in the circuit of 33–36.
views.N: Revelation 21:13 gives the new Jerusalem three gates on each side.
views.J: Ezekiel 48:31–34 also gives the city three gates on each side.
views.W: A short verse in Enoch's circuit of the world.

title: Enoch Blesses the Lord
sum: In the south Enoch sees three gates for the south wind, dew and rain. In the east he sees three gates with small gates above them, through which the stars pass west on their paths. Each time he sees these things, he blesses the Lord of glory, who has shown his great works to the angels and to human beings, so that they may praise his work and bless him forever.
readings: Read as the end of the Book of the Watchers
The journeys end in praise, as Psalm 104 does after its survey of creation.

views.E: Read as Scripture: all creation shows God's glory, and the right response is praise.
views.H: The closing blessing rounds off chapters 1–36. The Book of the Luminaries (72–82) takes up the same subject in detail.
views.N: Revelation 4:11 praises God as the Creator of all things.
views.J: Jewish blessings over the wonders of nature ("who does the work of creation") express the same response.
views.W: A doxology that most readers can share.

settings.when: at the end of his journeys
settings.why: To end the Book of the Watchers with praise for the Creator.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 200s BC, who knew Babylonian and Greek pictures of the world and placed God's judgment within it. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own journey, kept for the last generations.
